subject: Anthropology
title: The Silk Road
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Silk Road usable.

hook.text: Silk, spices, paper, and plague — all traveled the same routes from China to Rome for over a thousand years.

buildup.text: The Silk Road was a network of overland and sea routes linking East Asia, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe.

discovery.text: It spread Buddhism, Islam, and Christianity alongside goods. Trade routes are always idea routes too.

twist.text: There was no single road. It was a web of paths, oases, and middlemen. No one trader went the whole distance.

climax.text: The Silk Road shaped the medieval world. It connected civilizations that would have otherwise remained isolated.

punchline.text: Trade routes connect more than markets.

quiz.question: What traveled along the Silk Road besides goods?

details.summary: The Silk Road was a network of overland and maritime trade routes connecting China, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe for over two millennia. It facilitated the exchange of goods, religions, technologies, diseases, and ideas across the ancient world.
details.whyItMatters: The Silk Road demonstrates that globalization is not modern. Ancient civilizations were deeply interconnected through trade networks that transmitted Buddhism, Islam, plague, paper, and gunpowder across continents.
takeaways: The Silk Road connected China to Europe for over two millennia
It transmitted goods, religions, technologies, and diseases
It demonstrates that ancient globalization was extensive

faq.question: Was the Silk Road a single road?
faq.answer: No. It was a shifting network of routes across deserts, mountains, and seas. Multiple overland paths crossed Central Asia, and maritime routes connected China to Southeast Asia, India, East Africa, and Arabia. Few traders traveled the entire distance.

faq.question: What besides silk traveled along these routes?
faq.answer: Spices, gems, horses, paper, gunpowder, glass, and metals moved along with Buddhism, Christianity, Islam, and Manichaeism. Diseases including plague also spread along trade routes. The cultural transmission was arguably more significant than the material trade.
